title: The Big Bang and the Universe
seo_title: Year 10 Science: The Big Bang and the Universe Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Describe how the big bang theory models the origin and evolution of the universe and analyse the supporting evidence for the theory (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 10 science worksheets on the big bang and the universe: the big bang theory, red shift, Hubble's law, the cosmic microwave background, galaxies, the life cycle of stars and the origin of the elements. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Red shift and the cosmic microwave background are key evidence for the big bang.
body_html:
How to think about it

The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago and is still expanding.

  • Red shift: light from distant galaxies is stretched to longer wavelengths, so they are moving away. Further galaxies move faster (Hubble's law).
  • The cosmic microwave background is leftover radiation from the hot early universe.
  • The big bang made hydrogen and helium; stars made heavier elements by fusion and in supernovas.
Example

A galaxy's spectral lines shift towards red. Meaning?

longer wavelengths

Answer: moving away

Example

Where was the iron in your blood made?

fusion in a massive star

Answer: inside a star

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the big bang was an explosion at one point in space.
  • Thinking red shift means a star looks red.
  • Thinking all elements were made in the big bang.

faq.q: What evidence supports the big bang theory?
faq.a: Red shift of distant galaxies (the universe is expanding), the cosmic microwave background radiation, and the large amounts of hydrogen and helium in the universe.

faq.q: What is the life cycle of a star like the Sun?
faq.a: A cloud of gas and dust forms a main-sequence star, which becomes a red giant and finally a white dwarf. Massive stars explode as supernovas and leave neutron stars or black holes.

faq.q: How does Australia contribute to astronomy?
faq.a: Australia has radio telescopes such as Parkes and ASKAP and is helping build the Square Kilometre Array. First Nations peoples have one of the world's oldest astronomical traditions.

items.q: Which evidence supports this idea: “We see them as they were billions of years ago, when the universe was younger.”
c: Very distant galaxies look younger and less developed.
About 75% of normal matter is hydrogen and about 25% is helium.
The CMB has a temperature of about 2.7 K that is almost the same in every direction.
Almost every distant galaxy's light is redshifted.
items.e: Match the evidence to the idea.

items.q: Why is the CMB now in the microwave range?
c: The universe's expansion stretched the early light to much longer wavelengths.

items.q: What is a galaxy?
c: a huge system of billions of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity
items.e: We live in the Milky Way galaxy.

items.q: What does Hubble's law say?
c: A galaxy's speed away from us is proportional to its distance.

items.q: Why do radio telescopes such as ASKAP in Western Australia study the early universe?
c: Radio waves from distant hydrogen gas reveal the universe's history.
Radio waves come only from the Sun.
items.e: The Square Kilometre Array is being built in WA and South Africa.

items.q: Which elements were mainly made in the big bang?
items.e: Heavier elements were made later in stars.

items.q: What powers a star like the Sun?
c: nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
items.e: Fusion releases huge amounts of energy.

items.q: Evidence: The farther a galaxy is, the faster it moves away. What does it support?
c: This matches what the Big Bang model predicts for the first few minutes.
Space itself is stretching everywhere (Hubble's law).
This is leftover radiation from the hot early universe (the CMB).
items.e: Three main lines of evidence: redshift, the CMB and light-element abundances.

items.q: What is redshift?
c: light from an object moving away is stretched to longer wavelengths

items.q: Mia draws dots on a balloon and blows it up. All the dots move apart. What does this model?
c: the expansion of space carrying galaxies apart
items.e: No dot is at the centre.

items.q: What is the Big Bang theory?
c: The universe has always been the same.
Earth formed first, then the stars.
The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in a hot, dense state and has been expanding ever since.
A star exploded in the middle of space.

items.q: Jack plots galaxy distance against speed moving away. The points form a straight line through the origin. What does this show?
c: speed is proportional to distance (Hubble's law)
items.e: The slope is the Hubble constant.

items.q: What did Edwin Hubble discover in 1929?
c: More distant galaxies are moving away faster, so the universe is expanding.

items.q: Is the Big Bang an explosion into empty space from one centre?
c: No. Space itself expands everywhere at once.
Yes, from the centre of the universe.

items.q: Which elements formed mostly in the first few minutes after the Big Bang?
c: hydrogen and helium (and a little lithium)

items.q: Which evidence supports this idea: “This matches what the Big Bang model predicts for the first few minutes.”
c: Almost every distant galaxy's light is redshifted.
A faint microwave glow comes evenly from every direction in the sky.
About 75% of normal matter is hydrogen and about 25% is helium.
The CMB has a temperature of about 2.7 K that is almost the same in every direction.
items.e: Match the evidence to the idea.

items.q: Which evidence supports this idea: “This is leftover radiation from the hot early universe (the CMB).”
c: The farther a galaxy is, the faster it moves away.
Almost every distant galaxy's light is redshifted.
Very distant galaxies look younger and less developed.
A faint microwave glow comes evenly from every direction in the sky.
items.e: Match the evidence to the idea.

items.q: Kai says, 'The big bang was an explosion at one point in space.' What is a better description?
c: It was a bomb in space.
It was an expansion of space itself, everywhere at once.
It happened at the centre of the Milky Way.
items.e: There is no centre of the expansion.

items.q: Evidence: A faint microwave glow comes evenly from every direction in the sky. What does it support?
c: Space itself is stretching everywhere (Hubble's law).
The early universe was hot, dense and very uniform, then cooled as it expanded.
This matches what the Big Bang model predicts for the first few minutes.
This is leftover radiation from the hot early universe (the CMB).
items.e: Three main lines of evidence: redshift, the CMB and light-element abundances.

items.q: The 'Emu in the Sky' is seen in the Milky Way by many First Nations peoples. What is it made of?
c: dark dust clouds in the Milky Way
items.e: Its position helps tell the season for emu eggs.

c: They show the Earth is flat.
They come from mobile phones only.
They help measure matter spread between galaxies.
items.e: Scientific discoveries lead to new questions.

items.e: nebula → main-sequence star → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.

items.q: A star's spectrum shows strong iron lines. What can you infer?
c: It formed from gas that earlier stars had enriched with iron.
It is a Big Bang star.

items.q: In the life of a Sun-like star, what stage comes just before the main-sequence star stage?
items.e: nebula → main-sequence star → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf.

items.q: A spectral line at 500 nm in the lab is seen at 504 nm in a galaxy. What is the redshift z = Δλ ÷ λ?
Two radio engineers found a steady 'noise' from every direction in 1965. Why was it important?
c: It proved the universe is static.
It was the CMB, strong evidence for the Big Bang.

items.q: In the life of a Sun-like star, what stage comes just before the white dwarf stage?
items.e: nebula → main-sequence star → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf.

items.q: Why does the solar system contain heavy elements like iron and uranium?
c: It formed from gas enriched by earlier generations of stars.
They came from the Big Bang.

items.q: The Andromeda galaxy is blueshifted. Does this disprove expansion?
c: No, because blue is a kind of red.
No. Gravity pulls nearby galaxies together; distant galaxies still recede.

items.q: Why did scientists accept the big bang theory over the steady state theory?
c: The cosmic microwave background and red shift data supported it.
items.e: Theories change when new evidence is found.

items.q: A student claims the universe is not expanding because the solar system is not growing. What is the best reply?
c: Gravity holds the solar system together; expansion shows up between distant galaxies.
The solar system is growing fast.

items.q: Why do spectral lines of a distant galaxy match lab elements but appear shifted?
c: The galaxy is moving away, so the lines are redshifted.

items.q: In the life of a star more than about 8 times the Sun's mass, what stage comes just before the neutron star or black hole stage?
items.e: nebula → main-sequence star → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.

items.q: In 2017, astronomers saw two neutron stars merge and detected heavy elements. What did this show?
c: Neutron-star mergers make heavy elements like gold.

items.q: A spectral line is 400 nm in the lab but 390 nm in a galaxy's spectrum. What does this show?
c: blueshift: it is moving towards us

items.q: How does a raisin bread model show expansion?
c: As the dough rises, every raisin moves away from every other, faster for raisins farther apart.

items.q: Ella uses spectroscopes to look at light from a sodium lamp and the Sun. She sees matching lines. What can she conclude?
c: The Sun is made only of sodium.
items.e: Each element has its own spectral fingerprint.

items.q: In the life of a Sun-like star, what comes right after the main-sequence star stage?
items.e: nebula → main-sequence star → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf.

items.q: Why can't the age of the universe be less than the age of its oldest stars?
c: Stars are older than the universe.
The universe must have existed before any star formed in it.

items.q: Ruby compares absorption lines in light from a galaxy with lines from a lab. The galaxy's lines are shifted towards red. What does this mean?
c: The galaxy is moving away from us.
items.e: A blue shift would mean moving towards us.

items.q: A line at 500 nm in the lab appears at 505 nm in a galaxy's light. About how fast is the galaxy moving away? (v ≈ zc, c = 300 000 km/s)
Why are old stars mostly hydrogen and helium with few heavy elements?
c: They formed before many stars had made and spread heavier elements.
